series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] sched/numa: do not let the per-VMA PID filter gate promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) balancing mechanism, specifically related to VMA (Virtual Memory Area) scanning and promotion. The current implementation allows per-VMA PID filtering to gate promotion, leading to inefficient scanning and potential performance bottlenecks. The proposed changes modify the vma_is_accessed() function to allow scanning of rejected VMAs, promoting candidates from the whole address space while maintaining top-tier marking unchanged.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Addressed a reported issue where slow_only=false was set unconditionally, causing premature re-admission of VMAs. Proposed changes to patch 1 and 2 were outlined, with plans for a v2 next week after testing.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a memory tiering issue where read-only file-backed mappings are not being scanned in tiering mode, leading to inefficient page placement and unneeded rescanning. The patch introduces a new function `vma_is_ro_file` to identify such mappings and modifies the `task_numa_work` function to scan these VMAs with the slow_only restriction. This change ensures that only non-toptier folios are made hint-faultable, preventing unnecessary promotion of pages.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Addressed some concerns regarding unneeded rescanning, but acknowledged that there are still issues with concurrent scanners and ptl lock contention. Plans to push a v2 after additional testing.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Sep 04, 2026 at 02:20:06PM -0400, Gregory Price wrote:
> @@ -4302,7 +4316,7 @@ static void task_numa_work(struct callback_head *work)
>  		 * VMA can cause others to become "permanently unaccessed" if a scan
>  		 * cycle is consumed entirely by the large VMA.
>  		 */
> -		vma->numab_state->slow_only = false;
> +		vma->numab_state->slow_only = ro_file;
>  		if (!vma_pids_forced && !vma_is_accessed(mm, vma)) {
>  			if (!(sysctl_numa_balancing_mode &
>  			      NUMA_BALANCING_MEMORY_TIERING)) {

Sashiko thinks this causes unneeded rescanning, but I don't think it
does. The cursor prevents it from restarting, and when we loop back
around reset_ptenuma_scan() bumps the sequence.

It also had concerns about concurrent scanners and ptl lock contention,
but mm->numa_next_scan only admits one per scan period.

Either way on a rewalk the scan hits pte_protnone() and moves on.

~Gregory

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to stop VMA scan filters from gating promotion in the Linux kernel's scheduler and NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) subsystem. The current implementation applies a series of VMA-level filters before marking a VMA for hint faults, which can lead to issues with memory tiering. The patches modify the per-VMA PID filter and read-only file mapping exclusion to allow promotion candidates to be added without removing existing filters.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Addressed a double-put bug in fuse_try_move_page() and added an extra folio_get() before replace_page_cache_folio() to maintain the reference. Also, modified the per-VMA PID filter and read-only file mapping exclusion to allow promotion candidates to be added without removing existing filters.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/memory_hotplug: factor out node_is_memoryless()
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors the memoryless node check in mm/memory_hotplug.c by extracting it into a separate function, node_is_memoryless(). The existing check_no_memblock_for_node_cb() helper is also moved ahead of the add/online path for clarity. The patch introduces no functional changes.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about potential races between lockless read of node_spanned_pages() and ZONE_DEVICE memory hotplug, but did not request changes or object to the patch.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 02, 2026 at 03:55:07PM -0400, Gregory Price wrote:
> A memoryless node neither spans present pages (populated or ZONE_DEVICE)
> nor has an offline-but-added memory block still linked to it in sysfs.
> 
> try_offline_node() presently open-codes this memoryless check.
> 
> Pull that into a node_is_memoryless() helper and pull the existing
> check_no_memblock_for_node_cb() helper ahead of the add/online path
> so it's clearer what is happening here.
> 
> No functional change.
> 
> Signed-off-by: Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net>
> ---
>  mm/memory_hotplug.c | 60 +++++++++++++++++++++++----------------------
>  1 file changed, 31 insertions(+), 29 deletions(-)
> 
> diff --git a/mm/memory_hotplug.c b/mm/memory_hotplug.c
> index 226ab9cb078ad..d0e94057682af 100644
> --- a/mm/memory_hotplug.c
> +++ b/mm/memory_hotplug.c
> @@ -1491,6 +1491,36 @@ static int create_altmaps_and_memory_blocks(int nid, struct memory_group *group,
>  	return ret;
>  }
>  
> +static int check_no_memblock_for_node_cb(struct memory_block *mem, void *arg)
> +{
> +	int nid = *(int *)arg;
> +
> +	/*
> +	 * If a memory block belongs to multiple nodes, the stored nid is not
> +	 * reliable. However, such blocks are always online (e.g., cannot get
> +	 * offlined) and, therefore, are still spanned by the node.
> +	 */
> +	return mem->nid == nid ? -EEXIST : 0;
> +}
> +
> +/* Caller must hold the memory hotplug lock for this check. */
> +static bool node_is_memoryless(int nid)
> +{
> +	/*
> +	 * A node still spanning pages (especially ZONE_DEVICE) is not
> +	 * memoryless.  A node spans memory after move_pfn_range_to_zone(),
> +	 * e.g. once a memory block has been onlined.
> +	 */
> +	if (node_spanned_pages(nid))
> +		return false;

browsing sashiko feedback:

[Severity: High]
This is a pre-existing issue and was not introduced by this patch, but can
this lockless read of node_spanned_pages() race with ZONE_DEVICE memory
hotplug?

---

This seems legit and worth addressing (other notes are addressible as
well, but this is maybe noteworthy).

I actually have some old patches sandbagged that tried to marry the
ZONE_DEVICE hotplug pattern through mm/memory_hotplug.c rather than its
separare entry-point.  Might be worth a revisit.

I don't know that I want to predicate this particular fix on this patch
but it's worth a think.

~Gregory

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 0/2] mm/mempolicy: stop copying state in the interleave paths

version_history.subject: [PATCH 0/2] mm/mempolicy: stop copying state in the interleave paths

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm/mempolicy: use SRCU for the weighted interleave state
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces the current implementation of weighted interleave state management in the Linux kernel's memory policy module with a new approach using SRCU (Schedulable RCU) to pin the global iw_table object and use it in-place. This change allows for more efficient handling of concurrent updates to the weights, reducing the need for synchronization and improving performance. The patch also introduces a new mechanism for retiring the weighted interleave state, which involves calling SRCU for sleeping readers and kfree_rcu for reference-less ones. The changes were tested with various configurations and tools, including KASAN, PROVE_LOCKING, and DEBUG_OBJECTS_RCU_HEAD.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] mm/mempolicy: stop copying the nodemask in the interleave paths
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the unnecessary copying of a nodemask in interleave node selectors, which reduces memory usage and improves performance. The original copy was done to ensure consistency between the node count and the walk, but this is no longer necessary as bounds checking can be used instead. If an empty nodelist or weight is detected, the patch falls back to using numa_node_id(). This change affects several functions in the mm/mempolicy.c file, including weighted_interleave_nid() and interleave_nid(), which are used for allocating pages under a specific memory policy.

review_comments.author: Rakie Kim
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer pointed out that the patch's removal of read_once_policy_nodemask() may cause a potential issue in alloc_pages_bulk_weighted_interleave(), where the function derives per-node counts from a weight total summed over the mask, and a changing mask can make them exceed the request.

Reviewer Rakie Kim agreed that resolving the sleeping-allocation problem using SRCU is a better approach than patching the allocation site and removing copies from the fault path.

Reviewer Rakie Kim noted that after removing the nodemask copy, the loop bound in alloc_pages_bulk_weighted_interleave() no longer matches the actual mask being walked, which can cause the walk to stop short of the intended pages. They suggested counting nodes in the loop that sums weights, as done in weighted_interleave_nid(), to fix this issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello Gregory,

Thanks for the series.

On Fri, 28 Aug 2026 21:59:43 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

---

I went through both patches. Resolving the sleeping-allocation
problem with SRCU rather than patching the allocation site, and
removing the copies from the fault path along the way, looks like
the right direction to me.

---

I have a minor comment on this part. After this change, everything
else reads pol->nodes fresh at the point of use - the weight sum
and the walk both look at the current mask. Only nnodes is still
the count from this earlier read. If the mask changes in between,
the loop bound no longer matches the mask the loop is actually
walking, so the walk can stop short of the pages the weight total
planned for. Would it be better to count the nodes in the loop
that sums the weights, the way weighted_interleave_nid() does it
in this patch?

	nnodes = 0;
	for_each_node_mask(node, pol->nodes) {
		weight_total += table ? table[node] : 1;
		nnodes++;
	}

[...snip...]

Thanks again for your time.

Rakie Kim

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledges that the proposed solution to widen the SRCU window does not fix the issue and is unsure if it's worth the extra calculation, indicating a need for further revision.
sentiment_signals: author doubts the effectiveness of their own proposal
acknowledges the problem is not fully addressed

review_comments.author: Rakie Kim
review_comments.summary: The reviewer pointed out a potential issue where the policy mask can change between two reads of the nodemask, leading to inconsistent bounds and skewing the distribution during allocation. They suggested adding a counter to the sum loop to address this issue.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing Rakie Kim's concern about the patch causing incorrect distribution calculations due to the changing nodemask during a rebind operation. The author acknowledges that ensuring correct distributions would require locks or reworking the entire weight mechanism, and instead proposes keeping the change simple by cookieing the value that can cause a div/0 error.

review_comments.author: Rakie Kim
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that matching two reads of a changing nodemask does not guarantee a correct distribution, and agreed with the patch's approach to simplify by only bounds checking the walk.
review_comments.raw_body:
Fair enough. Your example makes the point. The mask can change after
the sum as well, so matching the two reads does not get us a correct
distribution either. Keeping it simple sounds right to me.

Please feel free to add the following to this patch:
Reviewed-by: Rakie Kim <rakie.kim@sk.com>

Thanks for walking through it.

Rakie Kim

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch eliminates unnecessary copies of nodemask and node weights in the interleave paths of the Linux kernel's memory policy module. It achieves this by using SRCU to pin node weights in place, operating directly on pol->nodes for nodemasks, and clamping the walk to a single pass. The changes improve performance but may introduce a small trade-off in distribution accuracy during rebind operations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/4] btrfs: split btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() into prealloc and commit phases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() function into three separate functions: prealloc, commit, and free. The prealloc phase allocates memory for a delayed node and item, populates the item data, and inserts it into an rb-tree. The commit phase reserves metadata space and performs the actual insertion. If the allocation fails, the free helper is called to release the allocated resources. This refactoring allows callers to handle ENOMEM errors before modifying on-disk state.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/4] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index before btree modification
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to pre-allocate delayed directory index space before modifying the btree. This change prevents ENOMEM failures from leaving the btree in a partially-modified state, which could only be resolved by aborting the transaction. The patch also introduces an optional parameter for callers to provide their own pre-allocated space, and removes a wrapper function that was no longer needed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/4] btrfs: handle ENOMEM from btrfs_insert_dir_item() without aborting
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to handle ENOMEM errors when inserting directory items without aborting the transaction. It adds -ENOMEM to the list of recoverable errors in btrfs_add_link() and updates btrfs_create_new_inode() to orphan newly-created inodes instead of aborting on ENOMEM. This change allows create(), mkdir(), mknod(), symlink(), and link() operations to return a graceful -ENOMEM error under memory pressure, preventing filesystem-killing aborts.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 4/4] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index for non-overwrite rename
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to the Btrfs file system that allows it to pre-allocate delayed directory index resources before making any btree modifications during a rename operation. This is done by introducing a new function, `btrfs_prealloc_delayed_dir_index`, which is called in the non-overwrite case of the `btrfs_rename` function. The patch also adds a new parameter to the `btrfs_add_link` function that allows callers to pass pre-allocated delayed directory index resources. This change aims to prevent ENOMEM errors from occurring after btree state has changed, by returning -ENOMEM early if the pre-allocation fails.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a long-standing issue in Btrfs where synchronous directory morphing operations can abort due to ENOMEM errors. The patches rework the code to perform memory allocations upfront, preventing aborts and ensuring data integrity.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 3/7] mm/page_counter: introduce per-page_counter stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-page_counter stock to improve the performance of memcg charge and limit checks. The current implementation uses per-cpu stocks, which can lead to expensive hierarchy walks and inefficient cache management. By pushing stock caches down to the page_counter level, each counter is responsible for its own charge, reducing the need for CPU-wide draining and improving scalability when adding new page_counters to a memcg.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 4/7] mm/page_counter: use stock in page_counter_try_charge

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 6/7] mm/memcontrol: convert memcg to use page_counter_stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch converts the memory cgroup (memcg) to use page_counter_stock, which transparently handles stock usage and refills. This change eliminates a special case in try_charge_memcg and removes the 7-memcg cap, allowing each CPU to cache an unbounded number of pages. The patch also enables draining stock on isolated CPUs and addresses a user-visible change for legacy cgroup v1 (memsw). Unused memcg code is removed, preserving obj_stock and FLUSHING_CACHED_CHARGE.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 7/7] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page_counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series introduces changes to the memcontrol subsystem in Linux, specifically focusing on the memsw page_counter. The goal is to improve the accuracy of memory accounting by giving memsw its own page_counter_stock, allowing it to benefit from caching charges like memory. This change addresses a previously introduced skew between memsw and memory charging.

review_comments.summary: Raised a concern about the change in do_memsw_account() being due to re-attaching the memory controller between v1 and v2 trees, which is not a common operation. Suggested guarding the v1 parts with !cgroup_on_dfl(memcg->css.cgroup).

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the per-cpu 'stock' from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing for more efficient and independent stock management. The stock is now a property of each counter rather than the CPU, eliminating the need for cross-memcg interference and random victim eviction. This change also enables transparent charging and refilling of stock through page_counter_try_charge(). As a result, multiple sources of stock management can be added to mem_cgroup without tightly coupling them to struct mem_cgroup.
